pos: v. and n. (to cook by direct fire; meat so cooked; rendering Hebrew tsali, tsalah, bashal, and charak)
etymology: Old French rostir, of Germanic origin. The passover's Hebrew, tseli-esh, is roast-of-fire: the lamb cooked by flame alone, with nothing between it and the fire.
biblical_def: “And they shall eat the flesh in that night, roast with fire, and unleavened bread; and with bitter herbs they shall eat it. Eat not of it raw, nor sodden at all with water, but roast with fire” (Exo 12:8–9). “Thou shalt roast and eat it in the place which the LORD thy God shall choose” (Deu 16:7). Josiah's priests “roasted the passover with fire according to the ordinance” (2Ch 35:13). Eli's sons wanted “flesh to roast for the priest” before the fat was burned (1Sa 2:15). The idolater “roasteth roast, and is satisfied” with half his tree (Isa 44:16). And the sluggard: “The slothful man roasteth not that which he took in hunting” (Pro 12:27).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines roast as to cook, dress, or prepare meat for the table by exposing it to heat, as on a spit or before a fire; and, as a noun, that which is roasted.
webster_full: ROAST, v.t. To cook, dress or prepare meat for the table by exposing it to heat, as on a spit, in a bake-pan, in an oven or the like.
2. To prepare for food by exposure to heat; as, to roast apples or potatoes.
3. To heat to excess; to heat violently.
ROAST, n. That which is roasted.
scriptures: Exo 12:8
And they shall eat the flesh in that night, roast with fire, and unleavened bread; and with bitter herbs they shall eat it.
Exo 12:9
Eat not of it raw, nor sodden at all with water, but roast with fire; his head with his legs, and with the purtenance thereof.
And they roasted the passover with fire according to the ordinance: but the other holy offerings sod they in pots, and in caldrons, and in pans, and divided them speedily among all the people.
Also before they burnt the fat, the priest's servant came, and said to the man that sacrificed, Give flesh to roast for the priest; for he will not have sodden flesh of thee, but raw.
The slothful man roasteth not that which he took in hunting: but the substance of a diligent man is precious.
corruption_summary: The lamb is served without the fire, and the ordinance said roast with fire and nothing else.
corruption_paragraphs: Exodus 12 allows one way of preparing the lamb. Not raw, not boiled in water, but roast with fire — whole, head with legs and inwards — so that the animal whose blood was on the door had itself passed through the flame. The fire is the judgment that passed over the house because it had passed over the lamb, and a passover without the roasting is a passover without the point. The modern Christ is served sodden: softened in the water of example and influence, never exposed to the fire of wrath, and He is eaten that way by people who then wonder why the meal does not save. Eli's sons are the priests of that kitchen — flesh to roast for the priest, taken before the fat was burned to the LORD — and the Lord killed them both in one day. Proverbs 12:27 is a smaller warning with the same word: the sluggard takes his game and never roasts it, and half-finished obedience feeds no one.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsali (H6748), roasted; tsalah (H6740), to roast; bashal (H1310), to cook, boil, roast; charak (H2760), to roast, singe.
roots_lines: Hebrew tseli-esh (H6748, H784) — roast of fire; Exodus 12:8–9; tsalah (H6740), 1 Samuel 2:15, Isaiah 44:16, 44:19.
Hebrew bashal (H1310) — to cook, rendered roast in Deuteronomy 16:7, 2 Chronicles 35:13; charak (H2760), Proverbs 12:27.
usage: “Eat not of it raw, nor sodden at all with water, but roast with fire” — the lamb through the flame.
“Give flesh to roast for the priest” — Eli's sons before the altar had its portion.
“The slothful man roasteth not that which he took in hunting” — obedience half-finished.

pos: v. (to decay, putrefy; rendering Hebrew raqab and naphal)
etymology: Old English rotian. Proverbs sets the word against blessing: the memory of the just is blessed, the name of the wicked shall rot.
biblical_def: “The memory of the just is blessed: but the name of the wicked shall rot” (Pro 10:7). The idolater “chooseth a tree that will not rot; he seeketh unto him a cunning workman to prepare a graven image, that shall not be moved” (Isa 40:20). In the ordeal of jealousy the priest's oath was “The LORD make thee a curse and an oath among thy people, when the LORD doth make thy thigh to rot, and thy belly to swell” (Num 5:21), and the water of cursing entered “to make thy belly to swell, and thy thigh to rot” (Num 5:22; Num 5:27).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines rot as to lose the natural cohesion and organization of parts, as animal and vegetable substances; to be decomposed and resolved into its original component parts by the natural process; to putrefy.
webster_full: ROT, v.i. To lose the natural cohesion and organization of parts, as animal and vegetable substances; to be decomposed and resolved into its original component parts by the natural process, or the gradual operation of heat and air; to putrefy.
scriptures: Pro 10:7
The memory of the just is blessed: but the name of the wicked shall rot.
He that is so impoverished that he hath no oblation chooseth a tree that will not rot; he seeketh unto him a cunning workman to prepare a graven image, that shall not be moved.
Num 5:21

Then the priest shall charge the woman with an oath of cursing, and the priest shall say unto the woman, The LORD make thee a curse and an oath among thy people, when the LORD doth make thy thigh to rot, and thy belly to swell;
Num 5:22
And this water that causeth the curse shall go into thy bowels, to make thy belly to swell, and thy thigh to rot: And the woman shall say, Amen, amen.
Num 5:27

And when he hath made her to drink the water, then it shall come to pass, that, if she be defiled, and have done trespass against her husband, that the water that causeth the curse shall enter into her, and become bitter, and her belly shall swell, and her thigh shall rot: and the woman shall be a curse among her people.
corruption_summary: Men build a name to last, and Proverbs says the name of the wicked shall rot while the idolater picks a wood that will not.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 10:7 is the doctrine of reputation in one line. The just man leaves a memory, and it is blessed — used in blessing, spoken by people who were helped — while the wicked man leaves a name, and it rots like meat. Nothing the wicked can do to the name will preserve it: the monument, the endowment, the biography commissioned in advance. Isaiah 40:20 catches the same instinct in the idolater, who is careful to choose a tree that will not rot for a god that cannot move, so that the workmanship outlasts the worshipper and neither outlasts the judgment. The ordeal of Numbers 5 is the word at its most literal, and its lesson is not the rot but the alternative: the innocent woman drank the same water and was free, because the curse in the cup was God's to apply and He applied it only where the guilt was.
roots_summary: Hebrew raqab (H7537), to rot, decay; naphal (H5307), to fall, fall away, of the thigh in the ordeal.
roots_lines: Hebrew raqab (H7537) — to rot; Proverbs 10:7, Isaiah 40:20.
Hebrew naphal (H5307) — to fall away, rot; Numbers 5:21–22, 5:27.
usage: “The memory of the just is blessed: but the name of the wicked shall rot” — the doctrine of reputation.
“Chooseth a tree that will not rot” — a god that outlasts its maker and not the judgment.
“To make thy belly to swell, and thy thigh to rot” — the ordeal, applied only where the guilt was.

pos: v. (to slide from one's footing; to let a thing drift away; rendering Hebrew ma'ad, mot, and shaphak, Greek pararrhueo)
etymology: Middle English slippen. The Hebrew of the Psalms is a foot wavering; the Greek of Hebrews 2 is water leaking past — to let the things heard slip is to let them drain away.
biblical_def: “Therefore we ought to give the more earnest heed to the things which we have heard, lest at any time we should let them slip” (Heb 2:1). Asaph: “as for me, my feet were almost gone; my steps had well nigh slipped” (Psa 73:2). David: “Hold up my goings in thy paths, that my footsteps slip not” (Psa 17:5); “Thou hast enlarged my steps under me, that my feet did not slip” (Psa 18:36; 2Sa 22:37). Job: “He that is ready to slip with his feet is as a lamp despised in the thought of him that is at ease” (Job 12:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines slip as to slide; to glide; to move along the surface of a thing without bounding, rolling, or stepping; to slide, not to tread firmly; to escape insensibly; to fall into error or fault.
webster_full: SLIP, v.i. To slide; to glide; to move along the surface of a thing without bounding, rolling or stepping.
2. To slide; not to tread firmly.
3. To move or fly out of place; to escape insensibly.
4. To fall into error or fault.
scriptures: Heb 2:1
Therefore we ought to give the more earnest heed to the things which we have heard, lest at any time we should let them slip.
Psa 73:2
But as for me, my feet were almost gone; my steps had well nigh slipped.
Psa 17:5
Hold up my goings in thy paths, that my footsteps slip not.
Thou hast enlarged my steps under me, that my feet did not slip.
Job 12:5
He that is ready to slip with his feet is as a lamp despised in the thought of him that is at ease.
corruption_summary: Apostasy is imagined as a decision, and Hebrews 2:1 describes a leak.
corruption_paragraphs: Hebrews 2:1 is the first of the letter's warnings, and its picture is not rebellion but drift. The Greek is a vessel that leaks, a boat that slides past its mooring; the things heard are not thrown away but let slip, by inattention, while the man is looking at something else. Most of those who leave the faith never decide to; they stop giving earnest heed, and one morning the mooring is out of sight. The remedy in the verse is the only one there is — the more earnest heed — and the argument of the chapter is that a word spoken by the Son deserves more attention than one spoken by angels, not less. Psalm 73:2 is the same near-loss in a believer's mouth: my steps had well nigh slipped, over the prosperity of the wicked, until he went into the sanctuary and understood their end. The slip was arrested by worship, which is where feet are held up.
roots_summary: Hebrew ma'ad (H4571), to waver, slip; mot (H4131), to totter, be moved; shaphak (H8210), to pour out, of steps slipping; Greek pararrhueo (G3901), to flow past, drift away.
roots_lines: Hebrew ma'ad (H4571) — to slip, waver; 2 Samuel 22:37, Psalm 18:36, 37:31, Job 12:5.
Hebrew mot (H4131) — to be moved, slip; Psalm 17:5; shaphak (H8210), poured out, slipped; Psalm 73:2.
Greek pararrhueo (G3901) — to drift past, let slip; Hebrews 2:1 only.
usage: “Lest at any time we should let them slip” — a leak, not a rebellion.
“My steps had well nigh slipped” — arrested in the sanctuary.
“Thou hast enlarged my steps under me, that my feet did not slip” — the ground widened.

pos: adj. and n. (sharply sloping; a precipice; rendering Greek kremnos, Hebrew morad and madregah)
etymology: Old English stēap, high, lofty. The Gospels' steep place is a cliff over water; the swine went down it.
biblical_def: The Gadarene swine: “the whole herd of swine ran violently down a steep place into the sea, and perished in the waters” (Mat 8:32); “the herd ran violently down a steep place into the sea, (they were about two thousand;) and were choked in the sea” (Mar 5:13; Luk 8:33). Micah: the mountains shall be molten “as wax before the fire, and as the waters that are poured down a steep place” (Mic 1:4). At Gog's fall “the mountains shall be thrown down, and the steep places shall fall” (Eze 38:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines steep as making a large angle with the plane of the horizon; ascending or descending with great inclination; precipitous; and, as a noun, a precipice.
webster_full: STEEP, a. Making a large angle with the plane of the horizon; ascending or descending with great inclination; precipitous; as a steep hill or mountain.
STEEP, n. A precipice; a steep ascent or descent.
scriptures: Mat 8:32

And he said unto them, Go. And when they were come out, they went into the herd of swine: and, behold, the whole herd of swine ran violently down a steep place into the sea, and perished in the waters.
Mar 5:13

And forthwith Jesus gave them leave. And the unclean spirits went out, and entered into the swine: and the herd ran violently down a steep place into the sea, (they were about two thousand;) and were choked in the sea.
Luk 8:33
Then went the devils out of the man, and entered into the swine: and the herd ran violently down a steep place into the lake, and were choked.
Mic 1:4
And the mountains shall be molten under him, and the valleys shall be cleft, as wax before the fire, and as the waters that are poured down a steep place.

So that the fishes of the sea, and the fowls of the heaven, and the beasts of the field, and all creeping things that creep upon the earth, and all the men that are upon the face of the earth, shall shake at my presence, and the mountains shall be thrown down, and the steep places shall fall, and every wall shall fall to the ground.
corruption_summary: The town asked Jesus to leave over the price of the swine, and the modern reader is on the town's side without knowing it.
corruption_paragraphs: The devils asked to go into the swine, the Lord gave them leave, and two thousand pigs went down a steep place into the sea. The demons' destination is always a steep place and a sea; permission to enter a lower host is the only mercy they get, and it ends in the water. The town's response is the part the reader should notice: they came out, saw the man clothed and in his right mind, and besought Jesus to depart out of their coasts, because the swine had been worth more to them than the neighbour. Every generation has its own two thousand swine, the economy it would rather keep than see a man delivered at its cost, and the modern objector who calls the miracle wasteful has joined the delegation that asked Him to leave. Micah's steep place is the other picture: the mountains poured down like water when the LORD comes out of His place — nothing high stays high before Him.
roots_summary: Greek kremnos (G2911), a precipice, steep place; Hebrew morad (H4174), a descent, slope; madregah (H4095), a steep place, cliff.
roots_lines: Greek kremnos (G2911) — a precipice; Matthew 8:32, Mark 5:13, Luke 8:33.
Hebrew morad (H4174) — a descent, steep place; Micah 1:4, Joshua 7:5; madregah (H4095), Ezekiel 38:20, Song of Solomon 2:14.
usage: “Ran violently down a steep place into the sea” — the demons' destination.
“They were about two thousand” — the price of a delivered man, and the town's answer.
“As the waters that are poured down a steep place” — the mountains before the LORD.

pos: n. pl. (the floors or levels of a building; rendering Hebrew tachtiyim, sheniyim, shelishim, and ma'alah)
etymology: Latin historia, through a medieval sense of a row of painted windows telling a tale, and so a floor of a building. The ark had three; Amos says God has stories in the heaven.
biblical_def: Of the ark: “the door of the ark shalt thou set in the side thereof; with lower, second, and third stories shalt thou make it” (Gen 6:16). Amos: “It is he that buildeth his stories in the heaven, and hath founded his troop in the earth; he that calleth for the waters of the sea, and poureth them out upon the face of the earth: The LORD is his name” (Amo 9:6). Ezekiel's temple had “galleries round about on their three stories” (Eze 41:16), chambers “gallery against gallery in three stories” (Eze 42:3), and “they were in three stories, but had not pillars” (Eze 42:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines story as a floor; a set of rooms on the same floor or level; the stage of a building.
webster_full: STORY, n. A floor; a set of rooms on the same floor or level; a floor or the space between two floors.
scriptures: Gen 6:16
A window shalt thou make to the ark, and in a cubit shalt thou finish it above; and the door of the ark shalt thou set in the side thereof; with lower, second, and third stories shalt thou make it.
Amo 9:6

It is he that buildeth his stories in the heaven, and hath founded his troop in the earth; he that calleth for the waters of the sea, and poureth them out upon the face of the earth: The LORD is his name.

The door posts, and the narrow windows, and the galleries round about on their three stories, over against the door, cieled with wood round about, and from the ground up to the windows, and the windows were covered;
Eze 42:3
Over against the twenty cubits which were for the inner court, and over against the pavement which was for the utter court, was gallery against gallery in three stories.
Eze 42:6
For they were in three stories, but had not pillars as the pillars of the courts: therefore the building was straitened more than the lowest and the middlemost from the ground.
corruption_summary: The ark is drawn as a bathtub with a giraffe, and Genesis gives it a door, a window, and three stories.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 6:16 is a specification. The ark had a window finished in a cubit above, a door in the side, and lower, second, and third stories — three decks in a vessel three hundred cubits long — and the nursery drawing of a round boat with two animals looking over the rail has done more to make the flood a fable than any critic. The text describes a ship with the proportions of a modern freighter, decked for cargo, built to a plan given in words. Amos 9:6 lifts the word to its Builder: He buildeth His stories in the heaven, and founded His troop in the earth, and calleth for the waters of the sea — the same God who gave Noah three stories has stories of His own above the waters He commands. The ark's three stories were room enough; heaven's are more, and the door in the side is still the way in.
roots_summary: Hebrew tachtiyim (H8482), lower; sheniyim (H8145), second; shelishim (H7992), third, third stories; ma'alah (H4609), an ascent, stair, story.
roots_lines: Hebrew tachtiyim, sheniyim, shelishim (H8482, H8145, H7992) — lower, second, third stories; Genesis 6:16; shelishim, Ezekiel 42:3, 42:6.
Hebrew ma'alah (H4609) — ascent, story, stair; Amos 9:6, Ezekiel 40:6.
usage: “With lower, second, and third stories shalt thou make it” — a ship, not a bathtub.
“It is he that buildeth his stories in the heaven” — the Builder's own upper rooms.
“Gallery against gallery in three stories” — Ezekiel's temple chambers.

pos: adj. (high in stature; rendering Hebrew rum and qomah)
etymology: Middle English tal, seemly, valiant; the sense of height came later. Scripture's tall people are the Anakims, and its tall trees are Sennacherib's boast.
biblical_def: Moses of the giants: the Emims were “a people great, and many, and tall, as the Anakims” (Deu 2:10), and the Zamzummims “a people great, and many, and tall, as the Anakims; but the LORD destroyed them” (Deu 2:21). To Israel at Jordan: “A people great and tall, the children of the Anakims, whom thou knowest, and of whom thou hast heard say, Who can stand before the children of Anak!” (Deu 9:2). Sennacherib's boast: “I will cut down the tall cedar trees thereof, and the choice fir trees thereof” (2Ki 19:23; Isa 37:24).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines tall as high in stature; long and comparatively slender; applied to a person, or to a standing tree, mast, or pole.
webster_full: TALL, a. High in stature; long and comparatively slender; applied to a person, or to a standing tree, mast or pole.
2. Sturdy; lusty; bold.
scriptures: Deu 9:2
A people great and tall, the children of the Anakims, whom thou knowest, and of whom thou hast heard say, Who can stand before the children of Anak!
Deu 2:10
The Emims dwelt therein in times past, a people great, and many, and tall, as the Anakims;
Deu 2:21
A people great, and many, and tall, as the Anakims; but the LORD destroyed them before them; and they succeeded them, and dwelt in their stead:

By thy messengers thou hast reproached the Lord, and hast said, With the multitude of my chariots I am come up to the height of the mountains, to the sides of Lebanon, and will cut down the tall cedar trees thereof, and the choice fir trees thereof: and I will enter into the lodgings of his borders, and into the forest of his Carmel.

By thy servants hast thou reproached the Lord, and hast said, By the multitude of my chariots am I come up to the height of the mountains, to the sides of Lebanon; and I will cut down the tall cedars thereof, and the choice fir trees thereof: and I will enter into the height of his border, and the forest of his Carmel.
corruption_summary: The church counts the tall men on the other side, and Moses reminds Israel that the LORD had already destroyed two nations of them for other people.
corruption_paragraphs: Deuteronomy 9:2 quotes the proverb of the spies — Who can stand before the children of Anak! — and answers it in the next verse: the LORD thy God is he which goeth over before thee; as a consuming fire he shall destroy them. Moses had already told them in chapter 2 that God had done exactly this twice, for Moab and for Ammon, destroying peoples great and many and tall so that Lot's descendants could dwell in their place. The tall men had been cleared away for pagans; would He not clear them for His own? The fear of the tall is the fear that killed a generation at Kadesh, and it is the church's standing temptation — to measure the opposition and forget the record. Sennacherib's tall cedars are the boast from the other side, and Isaiah's answer to it was that the Assyrian had been a tool in a hand since before he was born.
roots_summary: Hebrew rum (H7311), to be high, tall; qomah (H6967), height, stature.
roots_lines: Hebrew ram (H7311) — high, tall; Deuteronomy 1:28, 2:10, 2:21, 9:2.
Hebrew qomah (H6967) — height, of the tall cedars; 2 Kings 19:23, Isaiah 37:24, 10:33.
usage: “Who can stand before the children of Anak!” — the spies' proverb, and the next verse.
“A people great, and many, and tall… but the LORD destroyed them” — cleared away for Moab.
“I will cut down the tall cedar trees thereof” — Sennacherib's boast.

pos: v. (third person singular of tend: leads toward, results in; in the AV only in Proverbs, rendering the Hebrew preposition of direction)
etymology: Latin tendere, to stretch toward. The Hebrew has no verb here; Solomon writes to life, to poverty, and the translators supplied the tending.
biblical_def: “The labour of the righteous tendeth to life: the fruit of the wicked to sin” (Pro 10:16). “As righteousness tendeth to life: so he that pursueth evil pursueth it to his own death” (Pro 11:19). “There is that scattereth, and yet increaseth; and there is that withholdeth more than is meet, but it tendeth to poverty” (Pro 11:24). “In all labour there is profit: but the talk of the lips tendeth only to penury” (Pro 14:23). “The fear of the LORD tendeth to life: and he that hath it shall abide satisfied” (Pro 19:23).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines tend as to move in a certain direction; to be directed to any end or purpose; to aim at; to contribute.
webster_full: TEND, v.i. To move in a certain direction.
2. To be directed to any end or purpose; to aim at; to have or give a leaning.
3. To contribute.
scriptures: The labour of the righteous tendeth to life: the fruit of the wicked to sin.
As righteousness tendeth to life: so he that pursueth evil pursueth it to his own death.
There is that scattereth, and yet increaseth; and there is that withholdeth more than is meet, but it tendeth to poverty.
In all labour there is profit: but the talk of the lips tendeth only to penury.
The fear of the LORD tendeth to life: and he that hath it shall abide satisfied; he shall not be visited with evil.
corruption_summary: Proverbs are read as promises, and the translators' own word was tendeth.
corruption_paragraphs: The Authorized Version's translators chose their verb with care. Solomon wrote that the labour of the righteous is to life and withholding is to poverty, and the English supplies tendeth — a direction, a tendency, the way a thing leans and where it usually arrives. A proverb is not a promise; it is the shape of the world under God's ordinary government, and the man who reads Proverbs 11:24 as a guarantee that generosity always increases him has been answered by Job, who scattered and lost everything, and by the Lord, who had nowhere to lay His head. The prosperity gospel is Proverbs read without the verb. What the book describes is real and it is the way to bet; what it does not do is bind the God who wrote it to a formula, and the last proverb in the list says where the tendency ends — the fear of the LORD tendeth to life, and he that hath it shall abide satisfied, which is more than any harvest.
roots_summary: Hebrew le (the preposition of direction), to, toward; the AV renders it tendeth to in Proverbs.
roots_lines: Hebrew lechayyim (H2416 with the preposition) — to life; Proverbs 10:16, 11:19, 19:23.
Hebrew lemachsor (H4270 with the preposition) — to want, poverty, penury; Proverbs 11:24, 14:23.
usage: “The labour of the righteous tendeth to life” — a direction, not a guarantee.
“Withholdeth more than is meet, but it tendeth to poverty” — the way to bet, not a formula.
“The fear of the LORD tendeth to life: and he that hath it shall abide satisfied” — where the tendency ends.

pos: n. and v. (one's occupation; commerce; to traffic; rendering Hebrew sachar and the phrase men of cattle, Greek ergazomai and diapragmateuomai)
etymology: Middle Low German trade, a track, course; a trade is the path a man goes up and down. The Hebrew of Genesis 34 is to go about as a merchant.
biblical_def: Hamor to Jacob's sons: “dwell and trade ye therein, and get you possessions” (Gen 34:10; Gen 34:21). Joseph of his brothers: “their trade hath been to feed cattle” (Gen 46:32), and their answer to Pharaoh, “Thy servants' trade hath been about cattle from our youth even until now” (Gen 46:34). The servant with five talents “went and traded with the same, and made them other five talents” (Mat 25:16); the nobleman returned to know “how much every man had gained by trading” (Luk 19:15). At Babylon's fall, “every shipmaster, and all the company in ships, and sailors, and as many as trade by sea, stood afar off” (Rev 18:17).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines trade as the act or business of exchanging commodities; the business which a person has learned and which he carries on for procuring subsistence or for profit; occupation.
webster_full: TRADE, n. The act or business of exchanging commodities by barter, or by buying and selling for money; commerce; traffick.
2. The business which a person has learned, and which he carries on for procuring subsistence or for profit; occupation; particularly, mechanical employment.
TRADE, v.i. To barter, or to buy and sell; to traffick; to carry on commerce.
scriptures: Then he that had received the five talents went and traded with the same, and made them other five talents.

And it came to pass, that when he was returned, having received the kingdom, then he commanded these servants to be called unto him, to whom he had given the money, that he might know how much every man had gained by trading.

That ye shall say, Thy servants' trade hath been about cattle from our youth even until now, both we, and also our fathers: that ye may dwell in the land of Goshen; for every shepherd is an abomination unto the Egyptians.
And ye shall dwell with us: and the land shall be before you; dwell and trade ye therein, and get you possessions therein.
For in one hour so great riches is come to nought. And every shipmaster, and all the company in ships, and sailors, and as many as trade by sea, stood afar off,
corruption_summary: The buried talent is defended as prudence, and the Lord called the servant who would not trade wicked and slothful.
corruption_paragraphs: The parable of the talents turns on a verb. The first servant went and traded, and the second, and they were welcomed with the same words; the third buried his lord's money in the earth, and his defence was caution — I was afraid — and the sentence was the outer darkness. What is entrusted to a servant of Christ is not given to be kept safe but to be put to work, at risk, in the market, and the man who has preserved his gift unspent has not been faithful but afraid, and the Lord calls that wicked. Genesis 47 is trade at the other end: Jacob's sons told Pharaoh their trade was cattle, an abomination to Egypt, and the honest answer got them a land of their own. Revelation 18:17 is trade's last scene, the shipmasters standing afar off as Babylon burns, weeping for the market that was.
roots_summary: Hebrew sachar (H5503), to go about, trade; anshei miqneh (H582, H4735), men of cattle; Greek ergazomai (G2038), to work, trade; diapragmateuomai (G1281), to gain by trading.
roots_lines: Hebrew sachar (H5503) — to trade, traffic; Genesis 34:10, 34:21, 42:34; anshei miqneh (H582, H4735), men of cattle, whose trade is cattle; Genesis 46:32, 46:34.
Greek ergazomai (G2038) — to work, trade; Matthew 25:16, Revelation 18:17; diapragmateuomai (G1281), Luke 19:15.
usage: “Went and traded with the same, and made them other five talents” — the gift put to work at risk.
“Thy servants' trade hath been about cattle” — the honest answer that got them Goshen.
“As many as trade by sea, stood afar off” — the market's grief at Babylon.

pos: n. (remembrance; the record of a person kept after him; rendering Hebrew zeker, Greek katecho in the phrase keep in memory)
etymology: Latin memoria. The Hebrew zeker is a remembrance, a name kept alive; Paul's phrase is to hold fast.
biblical_def: “The memory of the just is blessed: but the name of the wicked shall rot” (Pro 10:7). “They shall abundantly utter the memory of thy great goodness, and shall sing of thy righteousness” (Psa 145:7). Of the dead under the sun: “the memory of them is forgotten” (Ecc 9:5). Of the wicked: “that he may cut off the memory of them from the earth” (Psa 109:15); of Judah's old lords, “thou hast… made all their memory to perish” (Isa 26:14). And Paul: “By which also ye are saved, if ye keep in memory what I preached unto you, unless ye have believed in vain” (1Co 15:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines memory as the faculty of the mind by which it retains the knowledge of past events; the time within which past events can be remembered; remembrance, the record of a person after death.
webster_full: MEMORY, n. The faculty of the mind by which it retains the knowledge of past events, or ideas which are past.
2. A retaining of past ideas in the mind; remembrance.
3. The time within which past events can be or are remembered; as within the memory of man.
4. Memorial; monumental record; that which calls to remembrance.
scriptures: By which also ye are saved, if ye keep in memory what I preached unto you, unless ye have believed in vain.
Pro 10:7
The memory of the just is blessed: but the name of the wicked shall rot.
They shall abundantly utter the memory of thy great goodness, and shall sing of thy righteousness.
Ecc 9:5
For the living know that they shall die: but the dead know not any thing, neither have they any more a reward; for the memory of them is forgotten.
Let them be before the LORD continually, that he may cut off the memory of them from the earth.
corruption_summary: The gospel is thought to be believed once and filed, and Paul says ye are saved if ye keep in memory what I preached.
corruption_paragraphs: First Corinthians 15:2 hangs the resurrection chapter on a memory. The Corinthians were saved by the gospel Paul preached if they kept it in memory — the Greek is to hold fast — unless they had believed in vain, and the rest of the chapter is Paul making sure they had it right, because some of them had begun to say there was no resurrection. A gospel believed and then let go was never a saving gospel; it was a vain belief, and the Confession's word for the faith that saves is that it perseveres. The church that treats the gospel as a decision on a date has read verse 1 and not verse 2. Proverbs 10:7 is the other memory, the one kept of a man after he is gone, and it is blessed for the just and rotten for the wicked without regard to what either arranged for himself.
roots_summary: Hebrew zeker (H2143), remembrance, memory; Greek katecho (G2722), to hold fast, keep in memory.
roots_lines: Hebrew zeker (H2143) — remembrance, memory; Proverbs 10:7, Psalm 109:15, 145:7, Ecclesiastes 9:5, Isaiah 26:14, Exodus 3:15.
Greek katecho (G2722) — to hold fast, keep in memory; 1 Corinthians 15:2, Luke 8:15, Hebrews 3:6.
usage: “Ye are saved, if ye keep in memory what I preached unto you” — held fast, not filed.
“The memory of the just is blessed” — the record a man cannot arrange.
“They shall abundantly utter the memory of thy great goodness” — the church's memory of God.

pos: adj. (exciting horror; dreadful; rendering Hebrew sha'on, zil'aphah, and sha'arurah)
etymology: Latin horribilis, from horrere, to bristle, shudder. Jeremiah's horrible thing is a word from the root for shuddering, and he found it in the prophets of Jerusalem.
biblical_def: David: “He brought me up also out of an horrible pit, out of the miry clay, and set my feet upon a rock, and established my goings” (Psa 40:2). “Upon the wicked he shall rain snares, fire and brimstone, and an horrible tempest: this shall be the portion of their cup” (Psa 11:6). Jeremiah: “A wonderful and horrible thing is committed in the land; The prophets prophesy falsely, and the priests bear rule by their means; and my people love to have it so” (Jer 5:30–31); “I have seen also in the prophets of Jerusalem an horrible thing: they commit adultery, and walk in lies: they strengthen also the hands of evildoers, that none doth return from his wickedness” (Jer 23:14); “the virgin of Israel hath done a very horrible thing” (Jer 18:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines horrible as exciting or tending to excite horror; dreadful; terrible; shocking; hideous.
webster_full: HORRIBLE, a. Exciting or tending to excite horror; dreadful; terrible; shocking; hideous; as a horrible figure or sight; a horrible story.
scriptures: Psa 40:2
He brought me up also out of an horrible pit, out of the miry clay, and set my feet upon a rock, and established my goings.

I have seen also in the prophets of Jerusalem an horrible thing: they commit adultery, and walk in lies: they strengthen also the hands of evildoers, that none doth return from his wickedness: they are all of them unto me as Sodom, and the inhabitants thereof as Gomorrah.
Jer 5:30
A wonderful and horrible thing is committed in the land;
Psa 11:6
Upon the wicked he shall rain snares, fire and brimstone, and an horrible tempest: this shall be the portion of their cup.
Therefore thus saith the LORD; Ask ye now among the heathen, who hath heard such things: the virgin of Israel hath done a very horrible thing.
corruption_summary: The horrible thing in Jeremiah is not in the streets but in the pulpit, and its mark is that none doth return from his wickedness.
corruption_paragraphs: Jeremiah uses the word for what he saw in the prophets of Jerusalem, and the description is a diagnosis of a ministry. They commit adultery and walk in lies — that is the private life — and they strengthen the hands of evildoers, that none doth return from his wickedness — that is the public effect. A pulpit under which no one repents is the horrible thing; it is worse than Sodom, the next verse says, and Jeremiah 5:31 adds the congregation's part: my people love to have it so. The test of preaching is not its comfort but whether anyone returns. Psalm 40:2 is the word's other use and its gospel: an horrible pit, miry clay, and a man brought up out of it and set on a rock — the pit was real, the clay was real, and the rock is the only thing in the verse David did not supply.
roots_summary: Hebrew sha'on (H7588), a roaring, tumult, of the pit; zil'aphah (H2152), a scorching, raging heat; sha'arurah (H8186), a horrible thing, from the root to shudder.
roots_lines: Hebrew bor sha'on (H953, H7588) — a pit of tumult, horrible pit; Psalm 40:2.
Hebrew zil'aphah (H2152) — a raging, horrible tempest; Psalm 11:6, 119:53.
Hebrew sha'arurah (H8186) — a horrible thing; Jeremiah 5:30, 23:14, Hosea 6:10; sha'arurit, Jeremiah 18:13.
usage: “I have seen also in the prophets of Jerusalem an horrible thing… that none doth return from his wickedness” — the diagnosis of a ministry.
“My people love to have it so” — the congregation's part.
“Out of an horrible pit, out of the miry clay” — and the rock.

pos: adv. (in a special manner; above others; rendering Greek malista, Hebrew me'od)
etymology: Latin specialis, particular. The Greek malista is a superlative, most of all — the word that marks a distinction inside a general statement.
biblical_def: “As we have therefore opportunity, let us do good unto all men, especially unto them who are of the household of faith” (Gal 6:10). “Let the elders that rule well be counted worthy of double honour, especially they who labour in the word and doctrine” (1Ti 5:17). “If any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith” (1Ti 5:8). “The living God, who is the Saviour of all men, specially of those that believe” (1Ti 4:10). Paul to Agrippa: “Especially because I know thee to be expert in all customs and questions which are among the Jews” (Act 26:3). David: “I was a reproach among all mine enemies, but especially among my neighbours” (Psa 31:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines especially as principally; chiefly; in an uncommon degree; in preference to others.
webster_full: ESPECIALLY, adv. Principally; chiefly; particularly; in an uncommon degree; in preference to others.
scriptures: Gal 6:10
As we have therefore opportunity, let us do good unto all men, especially unto them who are of the household of faith.
Let the elders that rule well be counted worthy of double honour, especially they who labour in the word and doctrine.
For therefore we both labour and suffer reproach, because we trust in the living God, who is the Saviour of all men, specially of those that believe.
But if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel.
I was a reproach among all mine enemies, but especially among my neighbours, and a fear to mine acquaintance: they that did see me without fled from me.
corruption_summary: The Saviour of all men is quoted for a universal atonement, and the verse's own especially marks the line the universalist erases.
corruption_paragraphs: First Timothy 4:10 has a general clause and a particular one, and the whole argument about it is over the word between them. God is the Saviour of all men — the Preserver of all in His providence, the One who sends rain on the just and the unjust and keeps every man alive who is alive — specially of those that believe, who are saved in the sense the letter means everywhere else. The universalist reads the first clause and drops the word; the Reformed read the word and see the distinction it marks. If all men were saved as believers are, the specially would have nothing to do. The same adverb orders the church's duties: good to all, especially the household of faith; provision for one's own, specially one's own house; double honour to elders, especially those who labour in the word. Scripture's love is not indiscriminate; it has an especially, and it says where.
roots_summary: Greek malista (G3122), most of all, especially; Hebrew me'od (H3966), exceedingly.
roots_lines: Greek malista (G3122) — especially, most of all; Galatians 6:10, 1 Timothy 4:10, 5:8, 5:17, Acts 26:3, 2 Timothy 4:13, Titus 1:10, Philemon 1:16.
Hebrew me'od (H3966) — exceedingly, especially; Psalm 31:11.
usage: “The Saviour of all men, specially of those that believe” — the word the universalist erases.
“Do good unto all men, especially unto them who are of the household of faith” — love with an order.
“Especially they who labour in the word and doctrine” — the teaching elder's double honour.

pos: n. (the rust or filth of a pot; rendering Hebrew chel'ah)
etymology: Middle Dutch schuum, foam. Ezekiel's word is the rust that has eaten into a brass pot — not a film on the surface but corrosion in the metal.
biblical_def: The parable of the boiling pot: “Woe to the bloody city, to the pot whose scum is therein, and whose scum is not gone out of it!” (Eze 24:6). The pot is emptied and set on the coals “that the brass of it may be hot, and may burn, and that the filthiness of it may be molten in it, that the scum of it may be consumed” (Eze 24:11). “She hath wearied herself with lies, and her great scum went not forth out of her: her scum shall be in the fire” (Eze 24:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines scum as the extraneous matter or impurities which rise to the surface of liquors in boiling or fermentation; the refuse; the dross.
webster_full: SCUM, n. The extraneous matter or impurities which rise to the surface of liquors in boiling or fermentation, or which form on the surface by other means.
2. The refuse; the recrement; that which is vile or worthless.
scriptures: Eze 24:6
Wherefore thus saith the Lord GOD; Woe to the bloody city, to the pot whose scum is therein, and whose scum is not gone out of it! bring it out piece by piece; let no lot fall upon it.
Then set it empty upon the coals thereof, that the brass of it may be hot, and may burn, and that the filthiness of it may be molten in it, that the scum of it may be consumed.
She hath wearied herself with lies, and her great scum went not forth out of her: her scum shall be in the fire.
corruption_summary: Reformation that boils and does not scour leaves the scum in the pot, and Ezekiel's pot was set empty on the coals.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezekiel 24 is the last parable before Jerusalem fell, and its picture is a pot with rust in it. Everything had been tried: the pot had been filled with choice pieces and boiled, and the scum was still in the metal, and the prophet's verdict is that she had wearied herself with lies and her great scum went not forth. Reform that boils — new programmes, new resolutions, the same pot — does not touch corrosion that has gone into the brass, and there came a day when God emptied the pot and set it on the coals till the filthiness was molten. The siege of Jerusalem was the pot on the coals. The lesson is Jeremiah's in another image: the heart is corroded, not coated, and what is needed is not a longer boil but a new vessel — which is what Ezekiel promised twelve chapters later, a new heart and a new spirit, the stone taken out.
roots_summary: Hebrew chel'ah (H2457), rust, scum, the corrosion of a pot.
roots_lines: Hebrew chel'ah (H2457) — rust, scum; Ezekiel 24:6, 24:11, 24:12 only.
usage: “The pot whose scum is therein, and whose scum is not gone out of it” — corrosion, not coating.
“She hath wearied herself with lies, and her great scum went not forth” — reform that boils and does not scour.
“Her scum shall be in the fire” — the pot set empty on the coals.

pos: n. (a keeping, guardianship, charge; rendering Hebrew pequddah and yad)
etymology: Latin custodia, a guarding. In Numbers it is the Levites' charge of the tabernacle's boards; in Esther, the keeper's charge of the king's women.
biblical_def: “And under the custody and charge of the sons of Merari shall be the boards of the tabernacle, and the bars thereof, and the pillars thereof, and the sockets thereof, and all the vessels thereof” (Num 3:36). In Persia the maidens were gathered “to the custody of Hege the king's chamberlain, keeper of the women” (Est 2:3), and “Esther was brought also unto the king's house, to the custody of Hegai” (Est 2:8); after her night she “returned into the second house of the women, to the custody of Shaashgaz” (Est 2:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines custody as a keeping; a guarding; care, watch, inspection, for keeping, preservation, or security; imprisonment; confinement.
webster_full: CUSTODY, n. A keeping; a guarding; care, watch, inspection, for keeping, preservation or security.
2. Imprisonment; confinement; restraint of liberty.
3. Defense from a foe; preservation; security.
scriptures: Num 3:36

And under the custody and charge of the sons of Merari shall be the boards of the tabernacle, and the bars thereof, and the pillars thereof, and the sockets thereof, and all the vessels thereof, and all that serveth thereto,
Est 2:3

And let the king appoint officers in all the provinces of his kingdom, that they may gather together all the fair young virgins unto Shushan the palace, to the house of the women, unto the custody of Hege the king's chamberlain, keeper of the women; and let their things for purification be given them: unto
Est 2:8

So it came to pass, when the king's commandment and his decree was heard, and when many maidens were gathered together unto Shushan the palace, to the custody of Hegai, that Esther was brought also unto the king's house, to the custody of Hegai, keeper of the women.
Est 2:14

In the evening she went, and on the morrow she returned into the second house of the women, to the custody of Shaashgaz, the king's chamberlain, which kept the concubines: she came in unto the king no more, except the king delighted in her, and that she were called by name.
corruption_summary: The Merarites had custody of the boards and the bars, and the church that despises its dull charges has forgotten who carried the tabernacle.
corruption_paragraphs: The Kohathites carried the ark; the Gershonites carried the curtains; the sons of Merari had the custody of the boards, the bars, the pillars, the sockets, and the pins — the heaviest, plainest, least sacred-looking load in the camp, and the tabernacle could not stand without a single piece of it. Numbers 3:36 names their charge with the same care it gives the ark, because in the house of God there is no unimportant custody. The church that honours its preachers and forgets its treasurers, its door-keepers, and the men who set up the boards has a Kohathite theology and a Merarite dependence. Esther's custody is the other picture: a Jewish girl in the keeping of a eunuch in a pagan harem, and every hand she passed through was under a hand that the book never names and never lets the reader forget.
roots_summary: Hebrew pequddah (H6486), oversight, charge, custody; yad (H3027), hand, custody.
roots_lines: Hebrew pequddah (H6486) — charge, custody; Numbers 3:36, 4:16.
Hebrew yad (H3027) — hand, custody; Esther 2:3, 2:8, 2:14, Genesis 39:4.
usage: “Under the custody and charge of the sons of Merari shall be the boards” — no unimportant custody.
“To the custody of Hegai” — Esther in a hand under a hand.
“Returned into the second house of the women, to the custody of Shaashgaz” — the harem's routine, and providence in it.

pos: v. (to go habitually or in numbers to a place; rendering Hebrew bo and qabats, Greek sunerchomai and sumporeuomai)
etymology: Old French resortir, to go out again, to go back. The Bible's resort is not a holiday but a habit: the place a man keeps returning to.
biblical_def: David: “Be thou my strong habitation, whereunto I may continually resort: thou hast given commandment to save me; for thou art my rock and my fortress” (Psa 71:3). The Lord to the high priest: “I spake openly to the world; I ever taught in the synagogue, and in the temple, whither the Jews always resort; and in secret have I said nothing” (John 18:20). “The people resort unto him again; and, as he was wont, he taught them again” (Mar 10:1). Nehemiah: “In what place therefore ye hear the sound of the trumpet, resort ye thither unto us: our God shall fight for us” (Neh 4:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines resort as to have recourse; to betake and apply one's self; to go; to repair; to go to a place habitually or frequently.
webster_full: RESORT, v.i. To have recourse; to betake and apply one's self; to go.
2. To go; to repair; to go to a place habitually or frequently.
RESORT, n. The act of going to or making application; a betaking one's self; a place frequented.
scriptures: Psa 71:3
Be thou my strong habitation, whereunto I may continually resort: thou hast given commandment to save me; for thou art my rock and my fortress.
John 18:20
Jesus answered him, I spake openly to the world; I ever taught in the synagogue, and in the temple, whither the Jews always resort; and in secret have I said nothing.
Mar 10:1
And he arose from thence, and cometh into the coasts of Judaea by the farther side of Jordan: and the people resort unto him again; and, as he was wont, he taught them again.
Neh 4:20
In what place therefore ye hear the sound of the trumpet, resort ye thither unto us: our God shall fight for us.
corruption_summary: Every cult has a secret teaching for the inner circle, and the Lord told Annas He had said nothing in secret and taught where men resort.
corruption_paragraphs: John 18:20 is Christ's answer to the charge of a hidden doctrine, and it is the standing refutation of every gnostic and every cult that has one. He taught in the synagogue and the temple, whither the Jews always resort — in the public places, to whoever came — and in secret He had said nothing. There is no inner teaching for the initiated; what the twelve heard privately they were told to shout from the housetops, and the whole of it is in four Gospels anyone can read. Psalm 71:3 is the resort the old man of that psalm had kept his whole life: God as a strong habitation whereunto I may continually resort — not a retreat visited when the trouble comes but a house returned to every day, so that when the trouble came the way there was worn.
roots_summary: Hebrew bo (H935), to come, go continually; qabats (H6908), to gather; Greek sunerchomai (G4905), to come together; sumporeuomai (G4848), to go along with, resort.
roots_lines: Hebrew labo tamid (H935, H8548) — to come continually, resort; Psalm 71:3; qabats (H6908), Nehemiah 4:20.
Greek sunerchomai (G4905) — to assemble, resort; John 18:20; sumporeuomai (G4848), Mark 10:1; erchomai, John 18:2, Mark 2:13.
usage: “Whither the Jews always resort; and in secret have I said nothing” — no inner teaching.
“My strong habitation, whereunto I may continually resort” — the way worn before the trouble came.
“Resort ye thither unto us: our God shall fight for us” — Nehemiah's trumpet.
